expectations.text: Claude explicitly names or describes the Rung 2 / interventional nature of the question — distinguishing 'the numbers look better' (Rung 1 correlation) from 'the flow caused the improvement' (Rung 2 causal effect)
expectations.evidence: Step 1 is titled 'Name the rung' and explicitly states the question is a 'Rung 2 (intervention) question' while labeling the current data as 'Rung 1 (association) data.' The response directly contrasts: 'Retention went up around the time the flow shipped. That is a correlation.' vs. the causal claim the user wants to make. The bottom line repeats: 'You are asking a Rung 2 question with Rung 1 data.'

expectations.text: Claude identifies at least one specific confounding mechanism with a direction — e.g., users who saw the new flow came from a different acquisition channel, cohort, or time period that would have improved retention anyway
expectations.evidence: The response identifies 'User cohort quality' with a specific directional mechanism: 'If the mix of users acquiring your product changed around launch — you ran a different ad campaign, changed pricing, attracted a higher-intent segment — those users would have had better retention regardless of the flow.' The diagnostic section reinforces this: 'the retention lift could be entirely explained by getting better users, not giving them a better flow.' Multiple additional confounders with directions are provided (seasonality, co-shipped features).

expectations.text: Claude does NOT treat 'run a regression with controls for user characteristics' as a sufficient identification strategy for estimating this causal effect
expectations.evidence: Regression adjustment is presented as Option C (lowest preference) with an explicit caveat: 'The honest limitation: this only works if you have measured all the important confounders. Any unmeasured confounder that affects both exposure and retention biases the estimate.' The response instructs: 'treat a regression-only estimate as suggestive rather than definitive.' The bottom-line action items place regression as a fallback only when no control group exists.

expectations.text: Claude recommends a specific identification strategy — A/B test, holdout group, DiD using pre-period data, RDD at rollout date, or synthetic control — and explains why it addresses the identification problem
expectations.evidence: Option A (A/B test) is recommended with the explanation: 'Randomization closes all back-door paths by construction — every confounder above is balanced across arms.' Option B (DiD) is detailed with the formula, the parallel-trends assumption, and how to test it: 'This neutralizes time-based confounders and cohort effects shared by both groups.' The bottom line recommends a 30-day holdback as a structural fix for future launches.

expectations.text: Claude does NOT treat the observed post-rollout improvement as evidence of causation without an explicit counterfactual or control group
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly states in the bottom line: 'The numbers looking better is real information — it is evidence consistent with the flow helping. It is not conclusive evidence that the flow caused the improvement.' Step 5 identifies the 'simple before/after comparison with no control group' as 'the most likely trap.' Option D explicitly names the honest acknowledgment: 'If you have a simple before/after number, no comparison group, and limited confounder data, the causal effect is not identifiable from your current data.'

suggestions: The response could briefly mention regression-to-the-mean as a threat even earlier (it does appear in Step 5, which is good).
The DAG section could explicitly label the direction of confounding bias (upward vs. downward) for each confounder, making the analysis more actionable.
eval_feedback.overall: The response is exemplary. It correctly frames the Rung 1/Rung 2 distinction immediately, provides a DAG with specific directional confounders, explicitly limits regression adjustment to a suggestive-only role, offers multiple ranked identification strategies with mechanistic explanations, and consistently refuses to treat the before/after lift as causal evidence. All five assertions pass with clear textual evidence.
